alt: Boltzmann distribution at one temperature with two activation energies: the catalysed Ea line lies to the left of the uncatalysed Ea line, so the area of the curve beyond it, the molecules with enough energy to react, is larger, while the curve itself is unchanged.
caption: Figure: a catalyst lowers Ea, so more molecules have enough energy; the distribution itself is unchanged

alt: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at two temperatures: both curves start at the origin and have the same area; the higher-temperature curve is lower and broader with its peak to the right, so the area beyond the activation energy Ea (the molecules able to react) is much larger.
caption: Figure: Boltzmann distributions at T₁ and a higher T₂; the area beyond Ea grows with temperature

alt: Born-Haber cycle for sodium chloride as an energy level diagram: from the elements at 0 the steps go up by +107 (atomisation of sodium), +494 (first ionisation energy of sodium) and +121 (atomisation of chlorine) to +722 kJ per mole, then down by 349 (electron affinity of chlorine) to the gaseous ions at +373, and finally down by 784 (lattice energy) to NaCl at −411, the same as the enthalpy of formation.
caption: Figure: Born-Haber cycle for NaCl (kJ per mole); the lattice energy is the step that completes the loop to ΔHf

alt: Cis and trans but-2-ene: in the cis isomer the two CH3 groups are on the same side of the C=C double bond (and the two H atoms on the other side); in the trans isomer the CH3 groups are on opposite sides. There is no rotation about the double bond, so they are different molecules.
caption: Figure: cis and trans isomers of but-2-ene; the double bond cannot rotate

alt: Shapes of four complex ions: [Ag(NH3)2]+ is linear with 180 degrees between the two ligands; [CuCl4]2- is tetrahedral at 109.5 degrees; cisplatin [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] is square planar with 90 degrees, the two NH3 next to each other; [Cu(H2O)6]2+ is octahedral with 90 degrees between neighbouring water ligands.
caption: Figure: linear, tetrahedral, square planar and octahedral complexes

alt: Energy diagram of d orbitals: in a free transition metal ion the five d orbitals have the same energy; in an octahedral complex the ligands split them into three lower and two higher orbitals with an energy gap ΔE. A photon of visible light with energy ΔE is absorbed when an electron moves up, so the complex appears coloured with the remaining wavelengths.
caption: Figure: d-orbital splitting in a complex; absorption of light across the gap ΔE gives colour

alt: Two graphs for a reversible reaction starting from reactants only: on the left the forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they meet and stay equal (dynamic equilibrium); on the right the reactant concentration falls and the product concentration rises until both become constant, at different values.
caption: Figure: at equilibrium the rates are equal and the concentrations stay constant (they need not be equal)

alt: The two enantiomers of lactic acid, CH3CH(OH)COOH: each has a central chiral carbon bonded to COOH, CH3, OH and H; the two molecules are mirror images across a dashed mirror plane, with OH on a wedge and H on a hashed bond, and cannot be superimposed.
caption: Figure: a chiral carbon with four different groups gives two non-superimposable mirror images

alt: Energy profile of an exothermic reaction: reactants at a higher energy than products; the catalysed path has a lower peak, so a smaller activation energy, but starts and ends at the same energy levels, so the enthalpy change is unchanged.
caption: Figure: a catalyst lowers the activation energy; reactant and product levels, and ΔH, are the same

alt: Energy profile for homogeneous catalysis: the uncatalysed route has one high peak; the catalysed route has two lower peaks with a dip between them for an intermediate, the catalyst reacting in step 1 and being regenerated in step 2, and both end at the same product energy.
caption: Figure: homogeneous catalysis gives a two-step route with two lower activation energies

alt: Concentration-time curve for a first-order reaction with half-life 345 s starting at 0.0800 mol per dm³: the concentration is 0.0400 at 345 s, 0.0200 at 690 s and 0.0100 at 1035 s, so every half-life is the same length, which proves first order.
caption: Figure: a first-order reaction has a constant half-life (345 s here)

alt: Hess cycle for the formation of propane from combustion data: carbon and hydrogen burn directly to 3CO2 and 4H2O with a total of −2326 kJ (3 × −394 plus 4 × −286), while propane burns to the same products with −2219 kJ, so the enthalpy of formation of propane is −2326 − (−2219) = −107 kJ per mole.
caption: Figure: energy cycle using combustion data; the enthalpy of formation is the difference between the two routes

alt: Boiling points in degrees Celsius of the hydrides of Groups 14 to 17 for periods 2 to 4: Group 14 rises steadily CH4 −162, SiH4 −112, GeH4 −88; but in Groups 15, 16 and 17 the period-2 hydrides NH3 (−33), H2O (100) and HF (20) are far higher than the next member, because of hydrogen bonding.
caption: Figure: boiling points of hydrides; NH₃, H₂O and HF stand out because they form hydrogen bonds

alt: Hydrogen bonding in water: the central water molecule forms four hydrogen bonds, two from its partially positive hydrogen atoms to the oxygen of molecules below, and two from the hydrogen atoms of molecules above to the lone pairs on its own oxygen.
caption: Figure: hydrogen bonds (dashed) between water molecules; each molecule can form up to four

alt: First ionisation energy across Period 3 in kJ per mole: Na 494, Mg 736, Al 577, Si 786, P 1060, S 1000, Cl 1260, Ar 1520. The general rise is interrupted by a dip from Mg to Al (the 3p electron is higher in energy than 3s) and a dip from P to S (the first paired 3p electron is repelled).
caption: Figure: first ionisation energies across Period 3, with the two dips explained

alt: Graph of log10 of the successive ionisation energies of sodium against the number of electrons removed: one electron is removed easily (494 kJ per mole), then eight electrons with slowly rising values from 4560 to 28 900, then a huge jump to 141 000 and 159 000 for the last two, showing the 2,8,1 shell structure.
caption: Figure: successive ionisation energies of sodium; each step up marks a new shell closer to the nucleus

alt: Four lattice types: a giant ionic layer with alternating Na+ and Cl- ions; a giant metallic lattice of positive ions with delocalised electrons between them; graphite as stacked layers with strong covalent bonds inside each layer and weak forces between layers; and diamond with each carbon bonded tetrahedrally to four others.
caption: Figure: ionic, metallic, graphite and diamond lattices (schematic)

alt: Mass spectrum of boron: a short peak at m/e 10 with relative abundance 19.9 and a tall peak at m/e 11 with relative abundance 80.1, giving a relative atomic mass of about 10.8.
caption: Figure: mass spectrum of boron; each peak is one isotope and its height is its abundance

alt: Mass spectrum of butanone (Mr 72): peaks at m/e 29 (abundance 15, C2H5+), 43 (100, the base peak, CH3CO+), 57 (8, C2H5CO+) and 72 (20, the molecular ion), so the highest m/e is the relative molecular mass and the tallest peak is not the molecular ion.
caption: Figure: mass spectrum of butanone; the molecular ion is at m/e 72 and the base peak at 43

alt: Mass spectrum pattern of chloroethane: molecular ion peaks at m/e 64 (C2H5 with chlorine-35) and 66 (chlorine-37) in the height ratio 3 to 1, the signature of one chlorine atom.
caption: Figure: one chlorine atom gives M and M+2 peaks in the ratio 3 : 1

alt: Sub-shell energy ladder for iron (26 electrons) drawn as orbital boxes with spin arrows: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s and 3p are full, 4s is full and sits slightly below 3d, and the five 3d boxes hold six electrons, one paired and four unpaired, giving 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6 4s2.
caption: Figure: electron configuration of iron in boxes; 4s is below 3d, and singly occupied boxes fill before pairing

alt: Schematic proton NMR spectrum of ethanol: a triplet for CH3 near 1.2 ppm with area 3, a singlet for OH near 2.6 ppm with area 1, and a quartet for CH2 near 3.7 ppm with area 2; the n + 1 rule gives the splitting, and TMS is the reference at 0 ppm.
caption: Figure: schematic proton NMR spectrum of ethanol (areas 3 : 2 : 1)

alt: Volume of carbon dioxide against time for 0.300 g of calcium carbonate with excess acid: the curve rises steeply then levels at 72 cm³, and a dashed tangent at t = 0 through (30 s, 54 cm³) has gradient 1.8 cm³ per second, the initial rate.
caption: Figure: gas volume against time; the tangent at t = 0 gives the initial rate (1.8 cm³ s⁻¹)

alt: Two graph panels for orders 0, 1 and 2. Concentration against time: zero order is a straight falling line, first order a curve with constant half-life, second order a curve that flattens more slowly. Rate against concentration: zero order is horizontal, first order a straight line through the origin, second order curves upward.
caption: Figure: concentration-time and rate-concentration graphs for zero, first and second order

alt: Measuring the standard electrode potential of copper: on the left the standard hydrogen electrode (platinum in 1.00 mol per dm³ H+ with hydrogen gas at 101 kPa bubbling over it) is connected through a high-resistance voltmeter and a salt bridge to a copper electrode in 1.00 mol per dm³ Cu2+; the voltmeter reads +0.34 V, the E standard of Cu2+/Cu.
caption: Figure: the standard hydrogen electrode (left) joined to a Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell; the reading is E⦵(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V

alt: Two reaction profiles for halogenoalkane hydrolysis: SN2 has a single peak at the transition state, with the reactants RX and hydroxide passing directly to products; SN1 has two peaks with a dip between them for the carbocation intermediate, and the first step, forming the carbocation, has the higher peak so it is the slow step.
caption: Figure: SN2 has a transition state; SN1 has a real intermediate and a slow first step

alt: pH against volume of base for 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol per dm³ acid and 0.100 mol per dm³ base: hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide starts at pH 1 and has equivalence at pH 7; ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide starts near pH 3 and has equivalence at pH 8.73; hydrochloric acid with ammonia has equivalence at pH 5.28. All three have equivalence at 25.0 cm³.
caption: Figure: three titration curves; the equivalence point is at 25.0 cm³ for each but at different pH values

alt: Titration curve of 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol per dm³ ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide: the half-equivalence point at 12.5 cm³ has pH 4.76, equal to the pKa; the phenolphthalein range 8.3 to 10.0 lies on the steep section near 25.0 cm³, while the methyl orange range 2.9 to 4.6 lies in the buffer region, so only phenolphthalein gives a sharp end-point.
caption: Figure: weak acid with strong base: pH = pKa at half-equivalence; the shaded bands are two indicator ranges

alt: TLC plate with solvent front 7.5 cm above the baseline: reference dyes P, Q and R have spots at 1.8, 4.2 and 6.0 cm (Rf 0.24, 0.56 and 0.80) and the mixture S has two spots at 1.8 cm and 6.0 cm, matching P and R, so S contains P and R but not Q.
caption: Figure: TLC plate for the food-colouring example; spots are compared by Rf on the same plate

alt: Six molecule shapes with bond angles: CO2 linear 180 degrees; BF3 trigonal planar 120 degrees; CH4 tetrahedral 109.5 degrees; NH3 pyramidal 107 degrees with one lone pair on top; H2O bent 104.5 degrees with two lone pairs; SF6 octahedral 90 degrees. Wedges come towards the viewer and hashed lines go away.
caption: Figure: shapes and bond angles from VSEPR; lone pairs are pairs of dots, which squeeze the bond angle

alt: Zinc-copper cell with a high-resistance voltmeter reading 1.10 V: a zinc electrode in 1.00 mol per dm³ zinc ions is the negative electrode where zinc is oxidised, a copper electrode in 1.00 mol per dm³ copper ions is the positive electrode where copper ions are reduced, a salt bridge joins the beakers and electrons flow through the wire from zinc to copper.
caption: Figure: the zinc-copper cell; electrons flow from the negative zinc electrode to the positive copper electrode
